definition: AI nationalism is the idea that nations should develop and control their own artificial intelligence technologies to advance their own interests and ensure technological sovereignty.
details: This concept is gaining traction globally, leading countries to implement new laws, form strategic alliances, and invest significantly in domestic AI capabilities.

explainer.lead: AI nationalism turns artificial intelligence into a strategic national asset that countries try to build, fund, and control at home. It matters because this outlook can shape chip exports, startup support, talent movement, and international cooperation, with consequences for both innovation and safety.

tiers.eli5: Imagine each country wants its own team, tools, and secret playbook for building very smart computer helpers, and worries that sharing them will let another team win. That is AI nationalism: countries try to grow and guard AI at home so it serves their own goals. It can create useful local technology, but treating everything as a race can also make countries less willing to cooperate.
tiers.practitioner: For engineers, this is a policy environment rather than an algorithm: national strategies and trade rules can affect chip access, cross-border talent, acquisitions, and which domestic suppliers or language technologies a project uses. A team may need to plan around available hardware and local regulations instead of assuming one global technology stack. Treating competition as permission to relax safety, or overlooking cultural bias in nationally tailored systems, are key pitfalls.
tiers.paperLevel: AI nationalism can be summarized as: national AI development + national control -> domestic interests and technological sovereignty, often justified by a zero-sum account of economic, political, and military advantage. Ian Hogarth's influential 2018 essay "AI Nationalism" predicted stronger government support for domestic AI alongside more closed economies and restrictions on acquisitions and talent movement. Its winner-takes-all framing has been linked to unsafe development and geopolitical tension, while critics such as Kerry McInerney argue that its rhetoric can reproduce historical racial and civilizational hierarchies.

explainer.example: In the United States, trade policies restricting China's access to critical microchips put the idea into practice: limiting a key input is intended to preserve a technological edge. The National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence similarly presents outpacing China in AI as important to national success.

explainer.intuition: The idea treats AI much like other strategically important capabilities: a country should not depend entirely on others for technology that may shape its economy, security, and political power. National control is presented as a way to protect domestic interests and technological sovereignty.
howItWorks: Identify AI as a source of economic, military, and geopolitical advantage.
Fund domestic research, startups, and national AI strategies.
Protect advantages through trade, acquisition, or talent restrictions.
Frame international AI development as a winner-takes-all competition.
Favor national priorities and local rules over unrestricted technology sharing.
explainer.whyItMatters: AI nationalism can direct investment toward domestic capabilities and technologies tailored to local languages and needs. Its zero-sum form also carries risks: unsafe AI development, geopolitical tension, military aggression, internet fragmentation, and systems that embed cultural biases.
misconceptions: It is not simply government funding for AI research; it links that support to national control, sovereignty, and rivalry.
It is not one international law or coordinated policy; strategies and restrictions vary by country.
It is not only an engineering issue; critics also connect its rhetoric to racism, imperialism, and civilizational stereotypes.
